subject: english-language
title: Crystal versus the Pedants
welcome_lead: David Crystal defends English in a thousand pages. Survey the descriptivist case for a healthy, changing language.
meta_desc: David Crystal's descriptivism and the prescriptivist-descriptivist debate at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have walked through Crystal's library — a thousand pages of healthy variation defended.

concepts.def: David Crystal's view that linguistics describes how language is used; change is healthy and normal.
The view that language should conform to fixed rules — rejected by mainstream linguistics but persistent in public debate.
Differences across regions, classes, ages and contexts — variation is the raw material of change.
Historical processes (Haugen's stages) by which one dialect becomes the standard.
Younger speakers leading change tend to consolidate the new form into the standard over time.
Crystal's term for the conventions of computer-mediated communication, a new third medium.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Crystal argues the linguist describes rather than prescribes. Worry about literally meaning figuratively is misplaced — speakers have used it that way for centuries.

He documents change to show its orderliness and creativity, defusing moral panic.

Einar Haugen's four-stage model — selection, codification, elaboration, acceptance — describes how one variety becomes the standard. English's standard emerged from the East Midlands dialect via Caxton's printing press.

Crystal frames internet English as conversation in writing: features such as initialisms and emojis serve real-time multimodal meaning.

Far from impoverishing literacy, the medium expands the repertoire.

mcqs.q: Is language change a sign of decline?
options: Language change only happens in informal speech, not in writing.
No — modern linguistics treats change as natural and continuous, not as decay. Every language has always been changing and will continue to.
Chomsky said children should be taught grammar from age two.
Language change shows that standards are falling and English is being ruined.
